overview: Wichita communities farmed, traded and defended settlements across the southern Plains. Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai histories feed into today’s Wichita and Affiliated Tribes. The map’s broad Kansas-to-Texas outline and 1492 start are imported coverage, not the borders or founding date of one kingdom. The living nation continues beyond the map’s 1783 cutoff.

periods.title: Villages and trading connections
periods.summary: Ancestral communities combined farming and bison hunting; Coronado encountered Quivira in 1541.

periods.title: Grass houses and defended towns
periods.summary: Village agriculture and seasonal hunting supported communities connected to neighboring Plains peoples.

periods.title: Displacement and imposed allotment
periods.summary: War, epidemic disease, removal, boarding schools and divided lands put families under severe pressure.

periods.title: Government and community renewal
periods.summary: Wichita and Affiliated Tribes maintained government, family networks and cultural work around Anadarko.

items.text: Trade linked Wichita ancestors with communities far beyond their fields. New Mexican pottery, turquoise and obsidian reached the Plains, while exchanges with Caddo communities brought valued bow wood and pottery. Horses, metal tools and guns later changed these networks, with Wichita traders also passing imported goods to Comanche partners.

A 2020 drone study examined an ancestral Wichita settlement near Arkansas City, Kansas, which some researchers identify with the Etzanoa visited in 1601. Thermal and multispectral images revealed a large circular earthwork beneath an apparently ordinary field. The authors compare it with council circles at other Great Bend sites; its precise purpose remains debated.

The same survey covered about 18 hectares and identified possible house basins as well as the circular feature. Heat differences and vegetation patterns helped researchers investigate buried structures without digging through the whole settlement. The study demonstrates how an archaeological landscape can survive beneath later land use.

In 2017, Wichita State student Mitchell Young found a Spanish horseshoe nail 87 centimeters down in an old storage pit at the proposed Etzanoa site. Archaeologist Donald Blakeslee suggested that its unbent condition suited an object traded rather than lost from a horse. That interpretation connects a tiny find with a much larger encounter.

In 1759, Taovaya and other Wichita defenders, with Comanche allies, resisted a Spanish expedition at the Twin Villages on the Red River. The Spanish force withdrew and left its two cannon behind. These communities could coordinate a formidable defense when an invading army threatened their settlements.

The fortified northern village combined a timber stockade with earthworks and a moat. Fields nearby produced maize, beans, pumpkins and watermelons. A town could therefore be both a busy agricultural center and a carefully engineered defensive position; food production and military strength were closely connected.

sections.title: At home and through the seasons

items.text: In the tribal history’s account of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, women planted corn, beans and squash. Beans climbed the cornstalks. Pumpkin strips were dried, woven into mats and folded for storage: a pantry item that could be rolled up. Food also went into hide bags in underground caches.

A grass house could accommodate ten to twelve relatives, including married daughters, their husbands and children. After returning from winter hunts, families repaired the houses. Women and boys climbed the cedar framework to attach bundles of bluestem grass, making spring repairs a family climbing project.

The year moved between village gardens and winter bison hunts. On the hunt, related families camped in tipis, and women sliced and dried meat for later use. Portable shelters and preserved food allowed households to travel while remaining connected to their farming villages.

The Wichita-Pawnee Visitation brings relatives and friends together through alternating hosts, meals, dances and gifts. The tribal account even includes cleaning the camp before departure. Hospitality involves both the memorable celebration and the practical work that makes a gathering possible.

sections.title: Survival, gathering and a living language

items.text: At Camp Holmes in 1835, Wichita representatives helped bring Comanche allies into a treaty recognizing rights to their homelands. Recognition did not prevent later dispossession. In 1863 Confederate forces drove Wichita people north into Kansas; without farmland, families endured hunger and epidemics before survivors returned to Indian Territory in 1867.

Government boarding schools punished Wichita children for speaking their language. Around the turn of the twentieth century, allotment broke reservation land into individual parcels and opened the remaining land to settlers. Tawakoni Jim and others resisted this assault on shared lands and village life.

Community gathering places helped families rebuild connections after allotment. Research with Wichita collaborators documents ichaskhah, a Camp Creek gathering ground near Anadarko used from the 1930s into the early 1960s. Families camped there for visits, meals, handgames and dances, and the gatherings also supported political decisions.

A small example from the tribe’s language-class dictionary is “so:ti:cʔa,” translated as “Thank you.” This is an attested modern teaching form of Wichita. It gives today’s readers a usable glimpse of the language that families and language workers are sustaining.

ending.text: The 1783 map cutoff is not the end of Wichita history. Despite war, removal, disease and allotment, Wichita and Affiliated Tribes continues as a living nation with government and community life centered near Anadarko, Oklahoma.
